catalog_quote: 2.4. Tone. Like all Chadic languages, Bade is a tone language. Words other than verbs have lexically specified tone patterns. Specific tone patterns associated with tense and other features determine verb tones. Nonethless, tone has a low functional load in Bade. The only pair of words that I have found in Western Bade that are clearly minimally distinct for tone is kàka 'grandparent' vs. kâka 'God'. Moreover, there are no morphological processes that do not have segmental distinctions in addition to tonal distinctions. Bade has a basic two-tone system, with grave accent marking low tone and absence of an accent marking high: ... (HH) 'four' ... (LL) 'six' ... (HL) 'ten' ... (LH) 'one'. A phonetic falling tone, marked by circumflex accent, is common. As is typical for Chadic languages, non-final falling tones can generally be taken as H+L compressed onto one syllable. ... new_statements.rule_in_words: Bade is a two-tone language (H, L; phonetic Fall, Rise and downstepped H; downdrift). No source opened says anything about word stress or accent: no stress rule, no statement that stress is absent or non-contrastive. The corroborating unpublished phonology chapter (Schuh n.d., Western Bade Phonology, p. 3) states 'Tone is phonemic in Bade, i.e. pitch relationships between syllables in words are fixed and non-predictable.. Western Bade can be analyzed as having only two phonemic tones: Hi Lo'.
new_statements.exceptions: None about stress. Nearest stress-adjacent remark: Schuh (Handout 04, 2002, p. 14; Western Bade Phonology fn. 3, p. 25) quotes Hyman (p.c. 1975) that many transcribed phrase-final 'downsteps' may be differences of intensity/duration rather than pitch — a phrase-boundary phenomenon, not word stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical word tone; citation forms of nouns in Western Bade end in high tone because of nunation (-n), which neutralises final tonal contrasts. Description is of Western Bade (Amshi); the 1978 SAL article and Ziegelmeyer's papers describe Gashua Bade, with the same two-tone system.
new_statements.identity_note: Schuh's descriptions (Kaye chapter, Western Bade Phonology ms, 2009 dictionary) are of Western Bade (Amshi/Dagona area); the 1978 SAL article, the 2004 Gashua dictionary and Ziegelmeyer's papers are of Gashua Bade. Glottolog 5.1 lists no separate glottocodes for Western, Southern or Gashua Bade under bade1248; the tone facts quoted hold across the dialects per Schuh.
